title: Arms held up (Exodus 17:8–13)
hook: when Moses tires, Aaron and Hur hold up his arms

segments.voice: Yesterday, manna: bread every morning, enough for one day, spoiled by morning if hoarded. Your line was daily bread.

Try this, if you can, right where you are: lift both arms straight out and hold them there. The first few seconds are easy. Give it a minute and the shoulders start to argue. Now stretch that to a whole afternoon, on a hilltop, in the desert sun, while below you a battle goes back and forth depending on whether your hands are up. That's Moses at a place called Rephidim. And his arms are getting heavy.
screen: `LIFT YOUR ARMS. HOLD THEM.` → `A HILLTOP AT REPHIDIM.` → `HIS ARMS GET HEAVY.`

segments.voice: First, the setup. Amalek, a desert people, attacks Israel on the road. Moses tells a man named Joshua to choose fighters and go out, a name this story will hear much more of. Moses climbs a hill with the staff of God in his hand, and two men go with him: his brother Aaron, and a man named Hur, about whom this story tells us nothing more. Second, the strange rule of the battle. Whenever Moses holds up his hands, Israel prevails. Whenever he lets them down, Amalek prevails. The text doesn't explain why. Third, the tiredness. Moses's hands grow heavy; he's no superhero. So Aaron and Hur put a stone under him, and he sits on it. Then they stand on either side, one on the left, one on the right, and hold up his hands. The Hebrew word for how his hands stay, steady until the sun goes down, is emunah, the word that elsewhere means faithfulness, even faith. His hands were faithful because his friends held them. Fourth, what Christians saw. Very early, writers like Saint Justin Martyr looked at Moses with his arms stretched wide and saw a figure of the cross: arms open, and the people saved. Catholics still see that posture every Sunday, when the priest raises his arms to pray the great prayers of the Mass on behalf of everyone there. The story is honest that this was a battle; Exodus doesn't make war pretty. What it holds up is something smaller and very human: even Moses couldn't do it alone.
screen: `JOSHUA FIGHTS. MOSES CLIMBS.` · `HANDS UP, ISRAEL PREVAILS.` · `A STONE, AND A FRIEND ON EACH SIDE.` · `ARMS OUTSTRETCHED: A FIGURE OF THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose arms are getting heavy right now: a parent of a newborn, a friend caring for a sick spouse, a teacher at the end of the term, a priest or a nurse running on empty. Aaron and Hur didn't fight the battle, but they brought a stone and stood on each side, so ask what your stone could be: a meal, a text, an afternoon of babysitting, a ride. If you pray, hold that person up before God; if you don't, keep them in mind.
Emunah, steadiness, faithfulness in Hebrew: the word for how Moses's hands stayed up, held steady by two friends until sunset. Today's word.
Your line: hold up their arms. A stone to sit on, and a friend on each side. That's day three hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: At Mass, the priest prays the collect and the Eucharistic Prayer with arms raised and open, the ancient orans posture, and early Christian writers saw in Moses's outstretched arms a figure of the cross.

fork.setup: you're Aaron on the hilltop. your brother Moses can't keep his arms up any longer, and the battle below is turning. what do you do?
options: take the staff and hold it up yourself.
tell him to rest and hope for the best.
find him a stone to sit on, and hold up one of his arms.
fork.reveal: they put a stone under him, and Aaron and Hur stand on either side holding up his hands until sunset. they don't replace him. they hold him up.

original.note: Hebrew: steadiness, faithfulness. in Exodus 17:12 it describes Moses's hands, held steady till sunset.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic trick that won a battle.
what it means: even Moses couldn't hold on alone, and two friends kept his arms up until the sun went down.
what a scholar hears: his hands were emunah, steady or faithful, and Justin Martyr read the outstretched arms as a figure of the cross.

chat.says: How did Moses keep his arms up all afternoon during the battle?
options: He didn't alone: Aaron and Hur sat him on a stone and held his hands.
He prayed so hard that God made his arms stop feeling tired.
Joshua ran up the hill between charges to hold them for him.
chat.meaning: Moses's hands grew heavy. Aaron and Hur gave him a stone and held up his hands, steady, emunah, until the sun went down.

Rephidim.meaning: the place where Israel fought Amalek

Amalek.meaning: a desert people who attacked Israel on the road

Hur.meaning: the man who held up Moses's other hand

Justin Martyr.meaning: an early Christian writer who saw the cross here

sources.ref: General Instruction of the Roman Missal (priest's posture at the collect and Eucharistic Prayer)

notes: 'Somewhere past eighty': Moses was eighty when he spoke to Pharaoh (Exodus 7:7); 'if you follow the Bible's numbers' hedges it.
Exodus 17:9 is the first mention of Joshua in the Bible: confirm.
Emunah in 17:12 ('his hands were steady'): confirm.
Justin Martyr, Dialogue with Trypho 90–91 (also Epistle of Barnabas 12) on Moses's outstretched hands as a type of the cross: confirm references.
The practice opens the hook with an arm-raising exercise ('if you can'); confirm it is accessible enough.
The war with Amalek is mentioned without detail; the later command against Amalek (17:14–16) is not taught here.
